title: Redwood structured output + function-calling demo - Novus Retail
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Novus Retail through structured output (JSON mode) and function/tool calling with schema enforcement and guardrails. Discussion covered reliability of JSON outputs, handling hallucinations, security (VPC, KMS, SOC 2), and POC next steps (benchmarks, POC env access, pricing). Customer asked about latency, batching, and how fallbacks work for schema violations.
action_items: Alex: send tailored pricing and POC statement of work by 2027-01-20
Priya: share demo notebook and sample schema templates (orders, inventory) by 2027-01-18
Jordan: provide sample prompt sets and CSV of expected response fields by 2027-01-22
Liam: confirm compliance requirements (data residency, audit window) by 2027-01-21
next_steps: Schedule POC kickoff (2-week bench + integration) - target week of 2027-01-25
Redwood to provision demo tenant with JSON mode enabled
Run 1k QPS simulation and share latency/cost report
Share security pack (SOC 2, ISO, SSO/KMS integration docs)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-15
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Novus Head of Platform), Maya Patel (Novus SRE), Liam O'Connor (Novus Security)

Summary (auto): quick demo of Redwood structured output JSON mode + function calling. Covered schemas, guardrails, error handling, performance tradeoffs, and next steps for a POC.

Topics: structured JSON outputs, schema validation, function/tool calling, streaming responses, latency vs batching, security (VPC/KMS/SAML), POC scope

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm alex with redwood, i'll kick us off. priya's our se and she'll run the demo.
[00:08] Jordan: hey alex, thanks. got the invite, excited to see the structured output stuff, we've been struggling with inconsistent json from models.
[00:15] Priya: great, yeah we'll show json mode, how we enforce schemas and then the function-calling hooks to call internal tools. we'll also talk about guardrails and how to detect and recover when the model deviates.
[00:23] Maya: quick context — we run data platform at novus, critical path is order enrichment and returns automation, latency target is sub-200ms p95 on reads, but we can batch for inference where acceptable.
[00:35] Alex: perfect, that's helpful. what scale are you seeing? qps, concurrency?
[00:40] Jordan: right now spikes ~400 rps during promos, baseline ~60. for the initial poc we probably want to simulate 1k qps to be safe.
[00:47] Priya: ok noted. couple quick qual questions: are you leaning towards hosted vs dedicated/private? and any data residency rules?
[00:55] Liam: security angle — we prefer private/vpc for production, need KMS/HSM integration and we've got EU-only data for some merchants. also SOC 2 is a must.
[01:06] Alex: redwood supports private deployment and we have k m s integrations, SOC 2 reports available; we'll send the security pack after the call.
[01:14] Jordan: great. show us the demo.
[01:17] Priya: switching to demo tenant — starting with JSON mode. so here's a sample prompt: 'extract order items, normalize SKUs, map to internal catalog, and return as strict JSON according to this schema.' i'll paste the schema — it's a json schema object (shows on screen). note: transcription sometimes munges schema characters but in the actual notebook it's intact.
[01:36] Priya: hitting run... streaming on — in JSON mode we validate tokens as they are generated against the schema and apply a token-level guardrail. if the model starts to stray we can either auto-correct, invoke a repair function, or fallback to a safe path.
[01:49] System / Speaker 4: (minor background noise)
[01:53] Priya: result coming in — generating... and you can see it's returning a strict JSON list of items: [ { "sku": "NV-12345", "qty": 2, "price": 12.99, "normalized_sku": "NOVUS-12345" }, ... ]
[02:10] Maya: that looks clean — but what about hallucinated fields or extra keys? we had models inventing fields before.
[02:16] Priya: good question. we have a schema enforcement layer. by default we drop unknown properties and can raise an error. for production you'd typically run a repair function — that's where function-calling comes in. you can register a function like 'repair_order_json' that will try deterministic normalization or flag for human review.
[02:33] Alex: and we surface these schema violations in the console and as traces so you can see frequency and examples.
[02:39] Jordan: whats the overhead of those checks? latency impact?
[02:43] Priya: minimal for single calls, maybe +10-30ms depending on complexity. bigger factor is whether you run a synchronous repair (adds a round trip) vs async background job. with batching you get better throughput but added latency.
[02:56] Jordan: you mentioned batching — how does batching interact with streaming and json mode?
[03:01] Priya: batching groups requests on the runtime; streaming is per-request so we interleave streams back to clients. in JSON mode we maintain per-request schema validation while still getting batching benefits for kernel execution. if you need strict p95 latency under 200ms we suggest small batch windows or dedicated capacity.
[03:20] Maya: any numbers we can look at? like p50/p95 on a 1k qps sim?
[03:25] Priya: our public benchmarks — on a dedicated pool with T4-like instances we see p95 ~180-220ms for 512 token context on optimized kernels, but real numbers depend on model, quantization, and sequence length. we'll run a bench for your workload and share the detailed report.
[03:42] Liam: what about model variants and fallbacks if capacity is constrained? we can't degrade to something that makes bad decisions.
[03:48] Alex: we support smart routing and fallback policies. you can define a policy to fallback to a cheaper model for non-critical tasks or to a deterministic rules engine. for critical order flows you can pin a high-accuracy model and enable canary rollouts.
[03:59] Jordan: show the function-calling flow.
[04:02] Priya: sure — switching to the function-calling demo. here we create a function definition in the platform: name, input schema, allowed outputs. the model can 'call' that function by emitting structured json that matches the function signature. when invoked, Redwood routes the payload to your specified webhook or internal tool.
[04:18] Priya: demonstrating: the model returns a call payload: { "function": "normalize_sku", "args": { "sku_raw": "N V 12345" } } — the platform then calls your endpoint, which returns canonical sku data, and we merge results back into the response.
[04:34] Maya: so we can enforce auth on the webhook?
[04:37] Priya: yes. webhooks support mTLS, signed payloads, and we can restrict endpoints to private VPC endpoints only (no internet egress).
[04:45] Jordan: if the model emits a malformed call, do you validate before invoking?
[04:49] Priya: yes — we validate against the declared input schema. malformed attempts are either rejected or passed to a repair function. we log every invocation and you can see the raw model trace in the console.
[04:59] Alex: also worth noting we can do replayable traces so you can re-run the exact tokens through a different model variant for debugging.
[05:06] Liam: ok, security — how are keys handled? KMS integration?
[05:10] Alex: we integrate with cloud KMS and HSM for private deployments. customer-managed keys are supported and audit logs include key usage. we'll include our KMS integration docs in the security pack.
[05:20] Jordan: any compliance attestations?
[05:22] Alex: SOC 2 Type II, and we support ISO certs. for private we can sign additional controls.
[05:29] Maya: latency again — if you do the repair function synchronously that adds an extra call to our systems. does redwood route that through your network or ours?
[05:36] Priya: you can choose: call can be executed in your VPC (private deployment) or our hosted env via secure webhook. for VPC-on-prem it's inside your network so latency is yours. if you want low-latency for critical paths we recommend dedicated capacity and colocated functions in your VPC.
[05:55] Jordan: what about retraining or tuning prompts? we want consistent mappings from raw text to normalized fields.
[06:00] Priya: Redwood Optimize helps — it suggests quantization profiles, batching settings, and prompt ensembles. we also integrate with evals so you can track regression on prompt sets. for mapping, we suggest a small labeled set to bootstrap a ruleset plus model-in-the-loop corrections.
[06:13] Jordan: can we push a validated mapping table into the runtime?
[06:16] Priya: yes — you can keep a deterministic mapping in your repair function or in a lookup table service that the function calls. the model can propose candidates but final write can be the deterministic table.
[06:26] Maya: about error cases — do you have built-in DL models for NER or do you rely on LLM only?
[06:31] Priya: customers do both. we host open models and you can deploy custom models. for critical NER we sometimes combine a smaller deterministic extractor plus an LLM for edge cases. Redwood doesn't force one approach.
[06:44] Jordan: how do we instrument costs? our finance team will want token-level breakdowns per route.
[06:49] Alex: Console shows token-level cost, model cost, and per-route dashboards. you can export granular reports. we'll share an example export in the POC.
[06:58] Jordan: any gotchas around schema enforcement and multi-turn chats? we have flows that probe the model across turns.
[07:04] Priya: in multi-turn, we maintain KV cache for history but for schema enforcement you usually validate the final output. we also support step-wise schemas — you can validate intermediate steps and block the flow on violations.
[07:18] Maya: does cache invalidation work when models update? e.g., you roll out a new model and some cached prefixes become invalid.
[07:24] Priya: good point — we version caches and recommend a rollout policy that invalidates caches for canary traffic or uses a cache TTL. Console surfaces cache hit rates and invalidations.
[07:36] Jordan: can you show a failure mode where the model ignores schema and how redwood handles it?
[07:40] Priya: sure — forcing a malformed response now... you can see the guardrail triggers and we auto-invoke the repair function. the console highlights the trace, shows the token that deviated, and marks the result as 'repaired' with a repair_score. note: transcription may blur the repair_score name.
[07:58] Alex: customers often want thresholds for automated repairs vs manual review; you can set policies per route.
[08:05] Liam: how do you prevent over-eager repairs that change business-critical fields?
[08:09] Priya: policy controls. you can restrict auto-repair to non-critical fields and require manual approval for price/discount changes. everything's auditable.
[08:20] Jordan: let's talk POC scope and success criteria. for us success is: 95% schema-valid outputs for orders, p95 latency <200ms for read paths, and <0.1% misnormalizations.
[08:33] Alex: that's clear. we'll put those into a SOW for the POC and run a 2-week bench where we replay your sample prompt set at varying qps.
[08:43] Priya: demoing integration now — showing a live function call to our repair endpoint, returning normalized sku. note the signed payload headers.
[08:55] Maya: small nit — the console view shows tokens sometimes truncated in the trace, is that a privacy thing?
[09:00] Priya: depending on retention policies, tokens can be obfuscated; there's a setting to redact sensitive fields automatically. we support PII redaction and token-level masking.
[09:12] Jordan: are we able to run this behind our SSO and restrict who can trigger repairs?
[09:16] Alex: yes, RBAC via SAML/SCIM is supported. we'll provision roles in the demo tenant for you to try.
[09:25] Liam: we require a 12-month audit log retention for certain merchants — is that configurable?
[09:29] Alex: yes, retention is configurable for enterprise customers; for hosted we offer tiers, for private it's configurable by you.
[09:36] Jordan: what's the path if we outgrow hosted — can we start hosted and move to dedicated or private?
[09:41] Alex: yes — same API and configs across modes. you can pin model versions and rollout policies remain unchanged; migration is mostly moving data plane. Redwood's platform abstraction is designed for that.
[09:52] Maya: back to function calling — does it support tool calling other than webhooks? like direct DB writes or calling internal lambdas?
[09:58] Priya: we support several handlers: webhooks, internal plugins (for private deployment you can register internal lambdas), and queued job handlers. for DB writes we recommend a controlled function that validates before writes.
[10:10] Jordan: will you share the demo notebook?
[10:12] Priya: yes — i'll share the notebook and some schema templates (orders, returns, inventory mapping).
[10:18] Jordan: ok pause — quick question from procurement: licensing model?
[10:21] Alex: for hosted it's usage-based per-token + per-embedding. for dedicated it's reserved capacity contracts, monthly/annual commits. we'll include pricing tiers in the SOW.
[10:31] Jordan: finance will push back if costs scale linearly. any cost controls?
[10:35] Alex: Optimize provides recommendations (batching, quantization) and Console gives token-level cost breakdowns so you can set budgets/quotas per route. you can also set auto-fallback to cheaper models for non-critical routes.
[10:49] Maya: show an example of quantization benefit for inference cost.
[10:52] Priya: quick slide — quantized model uses less memory, cheaper flops, ~30-50% cost reduction depending on accuracy hit. we'll run a quantization test during the POC.
[11:04] Jordan: can you commit to a test schedule? we'd like bench results within a week after kickoff.
[11:08] Alex: yes, typical bench run is 3-5 business days; we'll aim for a week to account for integration.
[11:14] Liam: what about data residency for EU merchants?
[11:17] Alex: can provision region-specific data planes; for private we can keep control plane on-prem if needed.
[11:24] Priya: demo continuing — showing rollouts: canary, A/B, automatic fallback. here's a canary policy that routes 10% traffic to new model and auto-falls back on error rate >1%.
[11:36] Jordan: useful. if fallback happens we want to know who to contact. can console send alerts?
[11:40] Alex: yes alerts via webhook, slack, email, and you can hook into pagerduty.
[11:46] Maya: an operational question — how do you handle model stateful caches (kv cache) for personalization?
[11:51] Priya: KV cache is maintained per-session and supports eviction policies; if you want persistence we can store serialized caches in your storage. cache versioning is supported to avoid staleness during rollouts.
[12:06] Jordan: can the repair function be a human-in-the-loop action?
[12:09] Priya: absolutely — you can push flagged items to a queue for review; reviewer accepts or rejects and that feedback can seed future prompt tuning.
[12:19] Liam: do you log reviewer changes for audit?
[12:22] Alex: yes, audit trail includes who changed what and when.
[12:27] Jordan: ok let's talk POC milestones quickly.
[12:30] Alex: milestone 1: provision demo tenant + sample data ingest. milestone 2: bench run + report. milestone 3: integration test with repair function. milestone 4: finalize SOW/pricing and discuss production timeline.
[12:44] Jordan: target prod in Q2 if POC goes well.
[12:47] Alex: good, we'll try to accelerate.
[12:50] Priya: last demo snippet — edge-case where model returns text instead of json; our parser catches it and we either auto-repair or mark for human review. showing console error trace now.
[13:06] Maya: ok that clarifies. any other questions?
[13:09] Jordan: only one — can we run a stress test with sample traffic containing intentional noise (bad skus, typos)? that's our main failure mode.
[13:16] Priya: yes, we'll include fuzzed inputs in the bench.
[13:19] Alex: action items recap — (reading from notes) we will send SOW and pricing, priya shares notebook and schema templates, jordan provides sample prompts and dataset, liam confirms compliance checklist.
[13:34] Jordan: thanks folks. Liam, Maya — anything from security/ops?
[13:38] Liam: just want the security pack and to run an architecture review before production.
[13:42] Alex: we'll schedule an architecture review with the solutions team — propose next week.
[13:47] Maya: thanks.
[13:48] Priya: wrapping up — i'll upload the demo notebook and share the tenant invite.
[13:52] Alex: cool thanks everyone. we'll send follow-up email with the SOW and schedule.
[13:58] Jordan: thanks all, bye.

--- End transcript ---

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (e.g., 'K V cache' vs 'KV cache', 'SAMEL' for 'SAML'), filler words present, speaker labels mostly correct though automated speaker diarization can swap names.
